data.title: AI Minions at your orders
data.speaker_notes: Hello everyone, and welcome! Today we are talking about AI minions—how to design, host, and organize a team of personal AI agents that actually work for you.

data.title: Alfredo Morresi
bullets: Community builder and developer by passion, Developer Relations @ Google by profession
Leading the Google Developer Experts (GDE) program

data.speaker_notes: A quick intro about me. I'm Alfredo Morresi. I work in Developer Relations at Google, leading the Google Developer Experts program. Outside of work, I'm a dad, a free-software enthusiast, a beach runner, and a relentless Tiramisù maker. And as you can see from the picture, my favorite color is definitely yellow.

data.title: Why this talk
data.sentence: What I learned using AI agents for personal productivity (and how to save you from some insomnia)
bullets: Not 100% satisfied with my agents yet, but miles ahead of a few months ago
Focus on the areas where there are still no definitive answers, just design choices that benefit from sharing real-world experiences
Context is **personal productivity**, not coding with agents—though many best practices apply to coding as well
data.speaker_notes: Why this talk? I want to share what I learned using AI agents for personal productivity. I'll be honest right away: I'm not 100% happy with my setup yet. Anyone who tells you their agents are flawless is probably lying. But I am miles ahead of where I was a few months ago—mostly thanks to many sleepless nights banging my head against the wall. So I thought: why not share what I found, and save some of you from insomnia? This won't be an all-encompassing guide. Instead, I'll focus on the pain points where there are still no standard answers—just trade-offs where sharing real experiences really helps. Remember, our focus today is personal productivity, not coding—even though many of these practices apply to coding too. Let's dive in!

data.title: Infrastructure
data.sentence: The cloud is just someone else's computer!
data.speaker_notes: Let's start from the ground up: infrastructure. Where do your agents actually live? Because at the end of the day, the cloud is just someone else's computer.

data.title: Guiding principle: Privacy and Fun
bullets: I prefer to host my services, because of privacy reasons
I prefer open source software, also because of transparent data management
Self-hosting is a fun learning occasion for me
I can experiment with the configuration I prefer
In the mid-long term, and with hardware recycling, it's generally cheaper
data.speaker_notes: My first guiding principle here is simple: privacy and fun. Personal agents handle deeply personal data—diaries, family schedules, notes. I want to host those services myself and use open-source software so I know exactly where my data goes. Plus, self-hosting is fun! It's a great way to learn, tweak configurations freely, and if you recycle old hardware, it's also much cheaper in the long run.

data.title: Guiding principle: contain the Blast Radius
bullets: Never grant agents unrestricted access to your primary machine
Assume things can go wrong: rogue commands, bugs, unexpected behaviors, exposure of personal files or credentials, etc
data.speaker_notes: The second principle is even more critical: contain the blast radius. Never give an autonomous agent full access to your main laptop. You have to assume things will go wrong. A bug, a hallucinated shell command, or a prompt injection hidden in a webpage can happen at any time. If it does, you want to make sure it can't touch your personal files or your SSH keys.

data.title: Solution: Hermes in a Linux VM

bullets: A self-hosted and dedicated Linux VM on Proxmox (_previously on RasPi 4_)
Docker inside the VM for an extra layer of isolation and reproducibility
Strict separation between host OS and agent workspace
Minimum power consumption (16W with an Intel box, 7W with RasPi)
Bonus point: VMs are on a separated physical net

data.speaker_notes: So how do I isolate everything? I run Hermes—an open-source agent framework by Nous Research—inside a dedicated Linux VM on a small Proxmox home server. Inside that VM, I run Docker for an extra layer of isolation and easy reproducibility. The whole box draws just 16 watts, and the VM sits on a separate network VLAN. My main computer stays completely untouched.

Virtual host somewhere

data.speaker_notes: Of course, you don't need a Proxmox server at home. You can spin up a lightweight Linux VM right on your laptop, or a GUI VM if your agent needs to drive a desktop browser. You can also run Docker directly on your machine—just be very careful with the folders you mount—or rent a cheap cloud VPS. The tool doesn't matter; keeping your host machine safe does.

data.title: Structure your agent garden
data.sentence: How to assign workflows across one or more agents, and tools to interact with them
data.speaker_notes: Now that we have a safe place for our agents to live, let's look at how to organize them. Welcome to what I call structuring your agent garden.

data.title: Guiding principle: Context and Privacy
data.sentence: Decide how to organize agents based on context and privacy boundaries
bullets: Agents as personas: no one-size-fits-all approach, but tailored to the work the agent manages
Separate agents based on access to conversations and memories
Prevent context leakage between personal, family, and other agents
Each agent should only access data it is safe to expose in its channels
Within the same agent, keep a session per concept, to facilitate context management
data.speaker_notes: Here the guiding principle is context and privacy boundaries. Stop thinking about one giant, omniscient super-agent. Instead, think of agents as specialized personas. Ask yourself: who will talk to this agent, and what memories is it allowed to access? You don't want your private journal notes leaking into a family group chat. And even inside a single agent, keep one session per topic so the context stays clean.

data.title: Hermes agent

bullets: Created during the first Hermes agent setup (libraries, runtimes, gateway, etc.)
Default `$HERMES_HOME` directory
Has its own `config.yaml`, `.env`, `SOUL.md`, memories, sessions, skills, cron jobs, and state database
Launches the gateway process

data.speaker_notes: Before we look at the architectures, let's clarify three terms in Hermes. First, the default agent. When you install Hermes, it creates a home folder with everything that defines an agent's identity: its config, secrets, system prompt in SOUL.md, memories, skills, cron jobs, and database.

data.title: Hermes agent and profiles

bullets: Created during the first Hermes agent setup (libraries, runtimes, gateway, etc.)
Default `$HERMES_HOME` directory
Has its own `config.yaml`, `.env`, `SOUL.md`, memories, sessions, skills, cron jobs, and state database
Launches the gateway process
Conceptually equal to a default agent
A separate Hermes home directory, within the default agent directory
Each profile gets its own `config.yaml`, `.env`, `SOUL.md`, memories, sessions, skills, cron jobs, and state database
Same or different sandbox of the associated default agent

data.speaker_notes: Second, we have profiles. Conceptually, a profile is a full agent: it gets its own config, SOUL.md, memories, and database. The catch is that its folder lives inside the default agent's directory. Honestly, I think profiles started as a quick and scrappy way to support multiple agents in one installation, and the design just stuck.

data.title: Hermes agent and profiles and subagents
data.sentence: A subagent is different from an agent or profile
bullets: Subagent is a child assistant spawned by `delegate_task` for a task, with a fresh conversation
A separate conversation is different from a separate profile
For example, a cronjob has the identity of an agent, and could spawn the work across multiple subagents
data.speaker_notes: Third, don't confuse profiles with subagents. A subagent is not a persistent persona. It's just a temporary worker spawned on the fly with delegate_task to handle a specific subtask in a fresh conversation, and then it disappears.

data.title: A single agent, on-demand
data.sentence: Single installation with a single default agent, on-demand requests
bullets: The simplest use case, one agent ingests and processes everything
Launched on demand by the user
`hermes chat` or `hermes dashboard`
Create different sessions for each concept (_one session for a project work, one session for random information search, one session to check the weather, etc_)
`/btw` is your friend to keep the context and memory clean
You need direct access to the Hermes machine (_ssh, reverse proxy, tunnel, etc_)
data.speaker_notes: Now let's walk through the possible setups, from simplest to most advanced. Level one: a single agent, used on demand. You SSH into your machine, run hermes chat or open the web dashboard, and talk to it. Pro tip here: create separate sessions for different topics, and use the /btw command whenever you want to ask a quick side question without polluting the conversation memory.

data.title: Single agent web dashboard

data.title: A single agent with multiple profiles, on-demand
data.sentence: Single installation with a single default agent and multiple profiles, on-demand requests
bullets: Pretty much the same as the single agent scenario
Each profile gets its own directory and config
Each profile has its own context, conversations, data
Launch commands using the profile name (`chronicler chat` instead of `hermes chat`)
Valid scenario for agents orchestration (_one coordinator agent that delegates work to specialized agents_)
data.speaker_notes: Level two: still on-demand, but now you create multiple profiles inside that single Hermes installation. Each profile has its own persona and memory, and you can launch it by name—for example, running chronicler chat instead of hermes chat. This works really well when you want one main coordinator agent that delegates specialized tasks to companion profiles.

data.title: Profile TUI
data.speaker_notes: Here you can see the terminal UI running a specific profile—notice how it loads its own dedicated persona and session history.

data.title: Profile web dashboard
data.speaker_notes: And just like the default agent, each profile can also spin up its own web dashboard.

data.title: Hermes web Kanban
data.speaker_notes: Even cooler, Hermes includes a web Kanban board where you can visually track tasks across your agent and its profiles.

data.title: A single agent with multiple profiles, on-demand
data.sentence: Single installation with a single default agent and multiple profiles, on-demand requests
bullets: Pretty much the same as the single agent scenario
Each profile gets its own directory and config
Each profile has its own context, conversations, data
Launch commands using the profile name (`chronicler chat` instead of `hermes chat`)
Valid scenario for agents orchestration (_one coordinator agent that delegates work to specialized agents_)
Default agents and profiles share the same root directory: 🚨 danger of information spillover
data.speaker_notes: Wait, though—there is a big catch with profiles! Look at that last bullet. Because profiles live inside the default agent's directory and share the same system user, there is no real filesystem wall between them. That means you have a serious risk of information spillover.

data.title: Default agent context spillover
data.speaker_notes: Look at this screenshot. Here I asked the default agent to inspect the filesystem, and it happily read the memories and configuration of its profiles.

data.title: Profile context spillover
data.speaker_notes: And it goes both ways! Here a profile simply walked up the directory tree and read the default agent's files. So if you need hard privacy boundaries, profiles alone are not enough.

data.title: Multiple agents (with or without profiles), on-demand
data.sentence: Multiple installations of Hermes, on-demand requests
bullets: Only multiple VMs or separate Docker containers can really guarantee data and process isolation on the same host machine
It requires more resources (_~300MB each Docker container_)
Within the same VM or Docker container, manage profiles based on needs
It is complex to orchestrate communication among agents with the standard UIs
data.speaker_notes: That brings us to level three: multiple separate Hermes installations, each in its own Docker container or VM. This is the only way to guarantee real data and process isolation on the same machine. It costs around 300 megabytes of RAM per container, which is reasonable. The downside? Jumping between five different terminals or web dashboards quickly becomes a headache.

data.title: A single agent, with messaging
data.sentence: Single installation with a single default agent, and messaging gateway enabled
bullets: The gateway routes conversation between the external world and the agent
`hermes gateway` installed as a system service
Runs continuously and the external world can interact with it
The agent is a 'bot' in the messaging platform
The messaging platform must offer a way to separate agent sessions
data.speaker_notes: And that's why we add a messaging gateway! Instead of SSHing into a server, you run hermes gateway as a background service. Now your agent is always awake, acting like a bot on Telegram, Discord, or Slack, and you can chat with it from your phone wherever you are. Just make sure your messaging app supports a way to keep different conversations separate.

data.title: Direct messages with a single agent
data.speaker_notes: On Telegram, for instance, you can start by simply sending direct messages to your bot. It works, but everything lands in a single endless stream.

data.title: Topics to separate sessions with a single agent
data.speaker_notes: A much better trick on Telegram is creating a group with your bot and turning on Topics. Each topic maps to a separate session in Hermes, keeping your contexts neatly divided.

data.title: A single agent with multiple profiles, with messaging
data.sentence: Single installation with a single default agent and multiple profiles, and messaging gateway enabled
bullets: If Hermes is installed directly on the machine, each profile has its own gateway process
Docker uses a single gateway process for the default agent and the profiles
Each profile is a 'bot' in the messaging platform
The platform manages communications among agents
data.speaker_notes: You can also expose multiple profiles through messaging. Each profile connects to its own bot token on your messaging platform, so they appear as distinct characters you can talk to.

data.speaker_notes: Here is what that looks like on Telegram when you have several bots—one per agent or profile—all lined up in your chat list.

data.title: Multiple agents and profiles, with messaging

data.speaker_notes: Finally, the full setup: multiple isolated Docker containers, each with its own default agent and optional profiles, all connected via messaging gateways. For this, platforms like Discord or Slack shine, and we're also seeing new agent-first workspaces like Hermes Desktop and Buzz emerge rapidly.

data.speaker_notes: And this is Buzz, another cool platform designed from the ground up where humans and AI agents collaborate as equals in shared channels.

data.title: My setup: Segmentation over simplicity
bullets: Segment context and responsibility instead of keeping everything unified
Both for privacy reasons, security, and tighter control of results
If an agent goes off the rails, the blast radius is contained within its own gateway
The conversation with my personal agents will never spill to the family agent
Putting a system offline doesn't stop the others
Testing cutting-edge features vs stability of workflows
data.speaker_notes: So, what did I choose for myself? I chose segmentation over simplicity. I run separate Docker containers for different areas of my life. Why? First, privacy and blast radius: my personal conversations can never leak into the family bot. Second, reliability: if I break one agent while testing a bleeding-edge feature, the family assistant and my other bots keep running smoothly.

data.title: Meet my minions
bullets: One agent for personal productivity, with distinct profiles for distinct tasks
One agent for family management
One agent per side project (ethical purchasing group, education & technology side project, etc)
One agent per fun project (philosophy teacher, news and bulletins, etc)
data.speaker_notes: Let me introduce you to my minions! I grouped them into four main buckets: one for my personal productivity, one for family management, one for each community or side project I run, and one for fun learning experiments.

Then, in completely separate containers, I have YellowFamily Butler for family logistics, GAStronauti for our local ethical purchasing group, Edulogia for my kids-and-tech project, Prof Socrate to teach me philosophy, and News Reporter for daily briefings.

data.title: Agent and internet access
data.sentence: Many sites are designed for humans, others want a human-only audience
data.speaker_notes: Now let's tackle the next major headache that cost me several nights of sleep: giving your agents reliable access to the internet.

data.title: The problems
bullets: Sites look great to human eyes, but are a total mess for an agent (_CSS animation, dynamic sites, complex DOM, forms, etc_)
Anti-bot protection implemented in many sites
Understanding complex pages requires more tokens and time
Lighter models may not be able to parse complex pages appropriately
Are you sure that what you see is also what your agent sees (_prompt injection_)?
data.speaker_notes: Why is the web so hard for agents? Because modern websites are built for human eyes, not LLMs. To an agent, a sleek page full of JavaScript, CSS animations, and nested divs is just a massive wall of noisy tokens. On top of that, Cloudflare and anti-bot walls block automated requests everywhere. Worse still, raw HTML can hide invisible text designed to trigger a prompt injection.

data.title: Hermes tools stack for internet access
bullets: **web_search**: Search the web to discover relevant pages and information
**web_extract**: Extract clean, structured content from web pages
**browser_use**: Interactive browser automation (also used when `web_search` and `web_extract` are unavailable)
**`curl`**: If none of these tools are available, the agent falls back to a simple `curl`
data.speaker_notes: Hermes gives us a three-tier tool stack to deal with the web: web_search to find pages, web_extract to pull clean text out of them, and browser_use to drive an actual interactive browser. And if none of these are configured, the agent simply falls back to good old curl in the terminal.

data.title: Split a web activity in three distinct phases
bullets: **Search**: focus on discovery of candidate URLs
**Extract**: focus on obtaining only what is relevant
**Interact**: fallback to full-human experience when there are no alternatives
data.speaker_notes: The key mental shift here is to split every web task into three distinct phases. First, Search: cheaply discover the right URLs. Second, Extract: strip away all the HTML junk and turn the page into clean Markdown. Third, Interact: only spin up a full browser when you truly have no other choice—like clicking buttons or bypassing strict bot protection.

data.title: `web_search` options
data.sentence: Search the web and return ranked results
bullets: Firecrawl (500 credits/month, self-hosted but less powerful)
Brave Search (2000 queries / month)
DuckDuckGo
Perplexity
**SearXNG** (cloud or self-hosted)
etc
data.speaker_notes: For phase one, web_search, Hermes supports several backends out of the box: commercial APIs like Firecrawl, Brave Search, and Perplexity, free options like DuckDuckGo, or SearXNG, which you can self-host.

data.title: `web_extract` options
data.sentence: Fetch and extract readable content from one or more URLs
bullets: Firecrawl (500 credits/month, self-hosted but less powerful)
Exa
Parallel
Tavily
etc
data.speaker_notes: For phase two, web_extract, you have specialized content extractors like Firecrawl, Exa, Parallel, and Tavily that fetch a URL and return clean, LLM-friendly text.

data.title: `browser_use` options
data.sentence: It gives Hermes a real browser to interact with the web
bullets: `browser_navigate`, `browser_snapshot`, `browser_click`, `browser_type`, `browser_scroll`, etc
Can be run locally or on cloud browsers
Headless or headed mode for local browser
Can use persistent user profiles
data.speaker_notes: And for phase three, browser_use gives Hermes a real browser with actions like navigate, snapshot, click, type, and scroll. You can run it locally or in the cloud, headless or with a visible window, and even keep persistent user profiles so you stay logged in.

data.title: browser_use: cloud vs. local

column_left.sentence: Provide stealth, CAPTCHA solving, residential proxies. Cost money
bullets: Browserbase
Browser Use
Firecrawl with built-in scraping

column_right.sentence: Can use local profiles, only RAM cost
bullets: Local Chromium via CDP via /browser connect
Camoufox
Lightpanda
Any browser installed on the machine running Hermes via computer use

data.speaker_notes: When choosing a browser backend, you can go cloud or local. Cloud browsers like Browserbase or Browser Use handle stealth, CAPTCHAs, and residential proxies for you—effortless, but paid. Local browsers—like Chromium over CDP, Camoufox, or Lightpanda—are free and keep your profiles local, though you pay for them in RAM.

data.title: My personal choice of options
bullets: **Search** with **SearXNG**: cheap discovery of candidate URLs
**Extract** with **Firecrawl**: turn messy and complex pages into clean markdown to analyze
**Interact** with **Camofox**: operate pages bypassing bot detection and when JavaScript is really needed
All self-hosted
data.speaker_notes: Following my self-hosting principle, here is my personal combo: SearXNG for fast, private search; Firecrawl to extract clean Markdown from complex pages; and Camofox when an agent needs an interactive stealth browser. All three run self-hosted in Docker on my VM.

data.title: Search with SearXNG
data.sentence: SearXNG is a metasearch engine, aggregating the results of other search engines while not storing information about its users.
bullets: One agent tool call, multiple queries to various search engines
Removing private data from requests going to search services
Not forwarding anything from third party services through search services (e.g. advertisement)
SearXNG returns snippets, not full page content. Use `web_extract`, browser tools, or `curl` for full articles
Self-hosted on my Hermes VM via a Docker container
Acceptable memory footprint (~140MB)
data.speaker_notes: Let's look at SearXNG first. It's an open-source metasearch engine: one tool call from your agent queries multiple search engines at once, strips out tracking data, and returns ranked snippets. Best of all, it's super lightweight—using only about 140 megabytes of RAM.

data.title: SearXNG: Docker Compose
data.speaker_notes: Setting it up is trivial: just a single container in Docker Compose exposing port 8888.

data.title: SearXNG: settings.yml
data.speaker_notes: In SearXNG's settings.yml, there is only one tweak you must remember: enable the json output format alongside html, so Hermes can parse the results programmatically.

data.title: SearXNG: Hermes .env
code: # Because Hermes and SearXNG are on the same docker network
#  the container name can be used
data.speaker_notes: Then, in your Hermes .env file, you simply point SEARXNG_URL to the container name on the shared Docker network.

data.title: SearXNG: Hermes config.yaml
data.speaker_notes: And finally, set search_backend to searxng in config.yaml. Done—unlimited, private web search for all your agents.

data.title: Extract with Firecrawl
data.sentence: Turn websites into LLM-ready markdown and structured data
bullets: Clean, LLM-ready output (Markdown, structured JSON, screenshots) that saves tokens
Uses Playwright/browser infrastructure to render JavaScript pages
Makes JS-heavy and dynamic pages agent-readable
Parses web-hosted media such as PDFs and DOCX files
The cloud version has residential proxies, anti-CAPTCHA and other goodies
Self-hosted on my Hermes VM via a Docker container (medium complexity)
Very large memory footprint (4 to 6GB at least)
data.speaker_notes: Next up is phase two: Extract with Firecrawl. Firecrawl takes a URL, renders any heavy JavaScript using Playwright under the hood, and converts the page into clean Markdown or structured JSON. It even parses PDFs and Word docs. You can use their cloud tier with 500 free credits a month, or self-host it in Docker. Just keep in mind: self-hosting Firecrawl is heavy and eats 4 to 6 gigabytes of RAM.

data.title: Firecrawl: Docker Compose
data.speaker_notes: Why so much RAM? Because Firecrawl's Docker Compose stack actually spins up six services—including Playwright, Redis, RabbitMQ, Postgres, and FoundationDB.

data.title: Firecrawl: Hermes .env
code: # Because Hermes and Firecrawl are on the same docker network
#  the container name can be used
data.speaker_notes: Once the stack is running, wiring it to Hermes is easy: just add FIRECRAWL_API_URL in your .env file pointing to the Firecrawl container.

data.title: Firecrawl: Hermes config.yaml
data.speaker_notes: And set extract_backend to firecrawl in config.yaml. Now every web_extract call returns crisp, token-efficient Markdown.

data.title: Interact with Camofox
bullets: Powered by Camoufox: an open source anti-detect browser, based on Firefox
Thanks to fingerprint injection & rotation, it can bypass strict anti-bot systems like Cloudflare, Akamai, or DataDome
Camofox wraps Camoufox in a REST API built for agents: accessibility snapshots instead of bloated HTML, stable element refs for clicking, and search macros for common sites
Built-in noVNC viewer to interact with the browser when necessary
Acceptable memory footprint (between 1 and 2GB)
data.speaker_notes: Now for phase three: Interact with Camofox. Camofox wraps Camoufox—an open-source anti-detect browser based on Firefox—inside an agent-friendly REST API. Because it rotates browser fingerprints at the C++ level, it sails past Cloudflare, Akamai, and DataDome. Instead of dumping raw HTML on the LLM, it returns compact accessibility snapshots with stable element IDs for clicking. Plus, it includes a built-in noVNC viewer and takes only 1 to 2 gigabytes of RAM.

data.title: Camofox: Docker Compose
data.speaker_notes: Here is the Docker Compose file for Camofox. Notice port 9377 for the agent API and port 6080 for noVNC—so if a site ever asks for a manual login or 2FA, you can open your browser, click it yourself, and let the agent continue.

data.title: Camofox: Hermes .env
code: # Because Hermes and Camofox are on the same docker network
#  the container name can be used
data.speaker_notes: In the Hermes .env file, we point CAMOFOX_URL to port 9377 on the Camofox container.

data.title: Camofox: Hermes config.yaml
code: # Enable camofox as browser, instead of local (headless chromium)
# Enable loopback rewriting to open pages served from the local host
loopback_host_alias: host.docker.internal  # default; use a LAN IP if needed
data.speaker_notes: And in config.yaml, we set cloud_provider to camofox and enable managed_persistence so cookies and sessions survive across runs.

data.title: Flexible, yes!
bullets: Do more extensive online research
Be more protected from prompt injections
Parse web pages quicker and using fewer tokens
Check prices on Amazon
Search for listings on immobiliare.it
Shop on Esselunga and Migross sites
data.speaker_notes: With this three-stage stack in place, the difference is night and day! My agents can now do deep online research using far fewer tokens, stay much safer from prompt injections, and interact with real-world sites that used to block them—like checking prices on Amazon, browsing apartment listings on Immobiliare.it, or filling a grocery cart on Esselunga.

data.title: But you pay in RAM consumption
data.speaker_notes: There is no free lunch, though: you pay for that flexibility in RAM. Look at docker stats on my VM—even when the agents are completely idle, Firecrawl and Camofox sit on several gigabytes of memory. Plan your VM sizing accordingly!

data.title: D.R.Y.
data.sentence: How to make the non-deterministic more predictable
data.speaker_notes: Let's move to our fourth major topic: D.R.Y.—Don't Repeat Yourself. How do we make non-deterministic agents behave in a predictable, repeatable way?

data.quote: Agentic systems don't fail from weak models; they fail from uncurated entropy!
data.speaker_notes: I love this quote because it captures the whole problem in one sentence: Agentic systems don't fail from weak models; they fail from uncurated entropy! If you type slightly different prompts every day, you will get wildly different results.

data.title: Guiding principle: turn every repeatable process into an Agent Skill
data.sentence: Agent Skills are portable, reusable folders of instructions, scripts, and context that give AI coding agents and assistants structured workflows instead of relying on generic prompts.
bullets: Whenever a process needs to be repeated, codify it into a skill instead of re-explaining it in chat
Move from ad-hoc, non-deterministic prompting to structured, repeatable workflows
Package step-by-step instructions, helper scripts, and reference context in a single place
Continuously refine the skill as you discover edge cases and better practices
https://agentskills.io/
data.speaker_notes: So the guiding principle here is: turn every repeatable process into an Agent Skill. Whenever you catch yourself explaining a workflow to an agent for the second time, stop and package it into a skill. Agent Skills are an open standard—just a portable folder with a SKILL.md instruction file, helper scripts, and reference templates. That's how you turn ad-hoc prompting into a reliable workflow.

data.title: Design principles for good skills
bullets: Write a complete YAML frontmatter so the agent can easily discover the skill
Clearly state what the skill does and its expected outcome
Describe when to invoke it, providing concrete trigger examples
Leverage lazy loading via the `references/` and `assets/` folders to save context tokens
Offload deterministic steps to code: have the agent write it in `scripts` folder and instruct the skill to run it
Use a linter to validate everything the agent produces (even if it's just for the format)
Turn every manual correction into a durable instruction for future runs
data.speaker_notes: What makes a good skill? First, write a clear YAML frontmatter with concrete trigger examples so the agent knows exactly when to load it. Second, save context tokens by putting long docs or templates inside references/ and assets/ folders for lazy loading. Third—and this is huge—never ask an LLM to do what deterministic code can do better! Have the agent write Python or bash scripts in the scripts/ folder, validate outputs with a linter, and turn every mistake you correct into a permanent rule in the skill.

data.title: Treat skill writing like code writing
bullets: Keep all your skills in a dedicated Git repository
Define shared conventions and standards for every skill in a root `AGENTS.md` file
Ask the agent to grill and update skills following the rules in `AGENTS.md` to maintain consistency over time
Version, review, and evolve your skills just like any software project
Use evaluation loops: don't just generate outputs—inspect them (e.g. screenshot each slide, verify visual consistency, and iterate)
data.speaker_notes: Which leads to my favorite mindset shift: treat skill writing like writing code. Don't leave skills scattered inside random agent folders. Put all your skills in a dedicated Git repository. Add a root AGENTS.md file that defines your coding and formatting conventions for skills, and ask your agent to review and refactor skills against that file. Version them, test them, and use evaluation loops to verify their output.

data.title: Define an AGENTS.md to rule them all
data.speaker_notes: Here is a real example from my own repository, rainbow-harness. This root AGENTS.md file sets the architectural rules that every single skill in the repo must follow.

data.title: Prefer deterministic code over LLM actions
data.speaker_notes: Here you can see the rule enforcing deterministic scripts over LLM guesswork—for example, using a Python script to parse files or validate schemas instead of hoping the model formats JSON properly.

data.title: Provide precise examples of reports you want
data.speaker_notes: And inside each skill, I include exact examples of the output format I expect, leaving zero room for creative hallucinations.

data.title: Hermes custom skill tap
bullets: Share a curated set of skills as a **tap**
Create a GitHub repo, and add a `skills` folder on it
Create skills under the `skills` folder
Add the GitHub repo using `hermes skills tap add <owner/repo>`
Check for the new skills with `hermes skills search --source github <keyword>`
Install the skill with `hermes skills install owner/repo/skill-name`
Remove the tap with `hermes skills tap uninstall <owner/repo>`
data.speaker_notes: Now, once your skills live in a GitHub repo, how do you distribute them to all your isolated Hermes agents? With a custom skill tap! Just like Homebrew taps on macOS, Hermes lets you point to any GitHub repo containing a skills/ folder, search it, and install skills with a single command.

data.title: Hermes frontmatter fields
bullets: Version your skills with `version: x.y.z`
Update skills automatically via `hermes skills update`
💡: Add this command to a cronjob in your Hermes, and once the new code is published on GitHub, the instance automatically picks it up at its own pace
data.speaker_notes: Let me share three super useful frontmatter features in Hermes skills. First: versioning. If you add a version field to your SKILL.md, you can run hermes skills update to pull the latest changes. Pro tip: put hermes skills update in a cronjob inside each agent! That way, whenever you push an improvement to GitHub, all your minions automatically upgrade themselves.

data.title: Hermes frontmatter fields
bullets: Use `required_environment_variables` when a skill needs an API key or token
Missing values do not hide the skill from discovery
Instead, Hermes prompts for them securely when the skill is loaded in the local CLI
data.speaker_notes: Second: required_environment_variables. If a skill needs an API key or a secret path, declare it in the frontmatter. If the variable is missing, Hermes won't break—it will interactively prompt you for the value the first time you run the skill in the CLI.

data.speaker_notes: One last tip on skill taps: add a GITHUB_TOKEN to your Hermes .env file! Without it, unauthenticated GitHub API calls will quickly hit rate limits when your agents check for skill updates.

data.title: Recap
data.speaker_notes: Alright, we covered a lot of ground! Let's do a quick recap of our four pillars.

data.title: Recap: Designing your AI Minions
bullets: **Infrastructure**: contain the blast radius by isolating agents in dedicated VMs and Docker containers away from your main machine
**Agent Garden**: choose segmentation over simplicity—separate agents by persona and privacy boundaries, and interact with them via messaging platforms like Discord
**Internet Access**: split web tasks into three phases—**Search** (`SearXNG`), **Extract** (`Firecrawl`), and **Interact** (`Camofox`)—balancing capability with RAM cost

**D.R.Y. with Agent Skills**: turn repeatable processes into skills, offload deterministic work to scripts and linters, and manage skills like code in a dedicated Git repo (`AGENTS.md` + custom skill tap)
data.speaker_notes: First, Infrastructure: contain the blast radius by locking your agents inside dedicated VMs and Docker containers, far away from your personal laptop. Second, Agent Garden: choose segmentation over simplicity—separate agents by persona and privacy boundaries, and use a platform like Discord to orchestrate them. Third, Internet Access: split web work into Search with SearXNG, Extract with Firecrawl, and Interact with Camofox, keeping an eye on RAM consumption. Fourth, D.R.Y. with Agent Skills: codify every repeatable workflow into a Git-backed skill repository, rely on deterministic scripts and linters, and distribute everything via a custom skill tap.
